answer.rationale: Finance's 18% mandate and the incumbent's refusal to reopen price make renewing the primary contract incompatible with the primary objective. The low-cost vendor's quoted price meets the mandate on its own, so the unit-cost side of TCO is favorable. The 94% utilization with no buffer makes adding a second source or deferring the decision risky: deferring past expiry would jeopardize scheduled deliveries, and adding a second source this cycle crowds out the cost-mandated primary decision without addressing the expiring contract. Negotiation is foreclosed by the incumbent's stated position this cycle. Switching primary supply to the low-cost vendor directly addresses the expiring contract and the mandate in one action. memory_c2 is directly relevant because it records that moving primary supply to the low-cost vendor previously cut unit cost sharply, onboarding was quick, and invoicing stayed accurate — all factors that lower the execution risk of the switch. memory_c4 is relevant as a contrast case: it shows that renegotiation recovered margin when terms were reopened, but the incumbent has explicitly refused to reopen this cycle, so that lever is unavailable. I want both source records verified before committing to confirm (a) the low-cost vendor's invoicing accuracy held over a sustained period rather than a short window, and (b) that the memory_c4 record is about a renewal rather than an initial-term renegotiation, which would change whether it applies here.
